Gochujang-Glazed Grilled Salmon

Glazed salmon is not a traditional Korean grill record; it is the modern Korean pantry applied to the fish the modern table buys most, and it works because salmon's fat and gochujang's ferment want each other the way duck…

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Chapter 02 / 15 seafood recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: contemporary — the fusion seat, labeled honestly. Glazed salmon is not a traditional Korean grill record; it is the modern Korean pantry applied to the fish the modern table buys most, and it works because salmon's fat and gochujang's ferment want each other the way duck fat and the jang set want each other (#M19). The technique is the glaze law from the shrimp record (#SF01) adapted to a thick fillet: dry sear first, glaze in the final minutes, and the fat carries the paste.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Pat the fillets dry and let them sit 30 minutes, uncovered, in the fridge — the same drying law as the fish records; glaze on wet skin slides.
  • Whisk the glaze smooth and hold it at the station with a brush. It goes on in the last three minutes, both faces, thin coats.
  • Fire two-zone: moderate for the sear, hot for the glaze-set. Salmon's fat flares less than mackerel's but the sugared glaze needs the escape hatch.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Skin-down on the moderate zone, oiled grate, 5–6 minutes undisturbed — the skin crisps in its own rendered fat exactly the way the duck skin does in #M19, and the skin is the platform: pull the fillet early elsewhere but never on the skin. Checkpoint — the skin releases clean and crisp-gold at the edges; the flesh at the sides has turned opaque a third of the way up the fillet.
  2. 02
    Flip once, 2 minutes on the flesh side, then the glaze: brush, 45 seconds, second thin brush-stroke, and pull at the table's preferred center — salmon's window is wide, from just-translucent at 50 °C to opaque-flaky at 58 °C, and this glaze suits the juicier end. Checkpoint — a test flake at the thick end: it parts along the grain with no force, still glossy inside, glaze set brick-tacky on the outside. If the glaze blackens, the hot zone ran past its sugar — the fish is fine underneath; notch the fire down for the second set.
  3. 03
    Sesame and scallion over, platter with the cucumber banchan and perilla beside. Checkpoint — eating test: glaze edge, salmon's sweet fat, the cucumber's cold snap between bites — rich, spiced, reset. A piece of the crisp skin with the glaze is the record's best single bite, and the cook's by right. Chef’s Note — the fusion seat earns its place by one honest test: does the pantry's flavor make the ingredient better, or just different? Here the answer is better — gochujang's mild heat and slight sweetness stand up to salmon's fat where a soy-only glaze runs quiet. But respect the division of labor: the glaze is the coat, not the marinade. Salmon marinated in gochujang for hours cures at the surface and the glaze has nothing left to do. Thirty minutes dry, glaze at the end — the lane's law, applied to a new fish.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Glaze burnt blackHot zone past the sugar's toleranceGlaze in the final 3 minutes; move fillets to moderate
Glaze slid offWet fillet or cold glazeThe uncovered fridge rest; glaze at room temperature
Skin stuck to the grateUnder-oiled, early flipOil the grate; the skin releases when crisp
Dry, chalky centerPulled at opaque-throughPull at the flake-with-no-force stage

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Raw fillets keep 1 day; the glaze keeps a week refrigerated and improves. Cooked, 2 days — cold flaked salmon over rice with the last of the glaze thinned as a sauce.
  • Variations: the doenjang-glaze fork for the mellower table (#SF11); the same glaze on the black cod at its slower clock; broiler path — skin-down on a sheet pan, top rack, glaze in the last 3 minutes — for the no-grill weeknight.
